opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think one of the things that's really exciting about AlphaFold 3 is that it's not just a protein structure predictor anymore. It's a model of how all of the molecules of life come together. So it handles proteins, but also small molecules, nucleic acids like DNA and RNA, ions, modified residues, and it predicts how they all interact in a single joint structure. That generality is what makes it relevant across very different therapeutic modalities.

If you think about small-molecule drug discovery, which is still the bulk of the industry, the key question is often: how does this ligand sit in the pocket of my target protein? AlphaFold 3 was a big step up there. On standard protein–ligand benchmarks it outperformed classical docking methods, and importantly it does that without needing an experimentally solved structure of the protein as input. That opens up targets where you don't have a crystal structure, or where the protein changes shape when the drug binds.

Then on the biologics side, antibodies and other protein therapeutics, you care a lot about protein–protein interfaces. Antibody–antigen interactions were historically quite hard for structure prediction, because there's not a lot of co-evolutionary signal to lean on. AlphaFold 3 made meaningful progress there, particularly when you sample more and use the model's own confidence measures to pick the best predictions. That's useful for understanding epitopes and for guiding design.

And then there are the newer modalities: RNA therapeutics, things like molecular glues and degraders where you've got a small molecule bridging two proteins, or gene-editing systems involving protein–nucleic acid complexes. Those are exactly the cases where you need to model multiple different kinds of molecules at once, and that's where having one unified model really pays off.

I'd be honest that it's not a solved problem in every modality. Accuracy varies, and things like dynamics, binding affinity, and very flexible systems are still open challenges. But the way we think about it, especially at Isomorphic, is that AlphaFold 3 is a foundation. It gives you a general understanding of molecular interactions, and then you build on top of it, combining it with other models and with experimental data, to actually design drugs across whichever modality makes the most sense for a given disease.

r001.rationale: The response describes AlphaFold 3 modeling small-molecule ligands in target-protein pockets and antibody–antigen interactions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the things that's really exciting about AlphaFold 3, and really the direction we've been pushing at Isomorphic. If you look at AlphaFold 2, it was incredibly powerful, but it was fundamentally a protein structure prediction model. It took an amino acid sequence and gave you the fold. Which is amazing, but when you're actually doing drug discovery, the protein on its own is only part of the picture. What you really care about is how that protein interacts with other things: small molecules, other proteins, nucleic acids, ions, post-translational modifications, all of that.

So with AlphaFold 3 we deliberately went for a much more general model. It takes the full set of biomolecular components in a complex and predicts the joint structure. And the reason that matters across modalities is that the modalities are really just different kinds of interactions. If you're working on a small molecule program, the key question is how does this ligand sit in the binding pocket, what's the pose, what's driving the affinity. If you're working on a biologic, an antibody say, the question is where does it bind on the antigen, what's the epitope and paratope, and how does that interface look. If you're thinking about something like a molecular glue or a degrader, you're now asking about a ternary complex, two proteins and a small molecule all coming together. And one model that can reason about all of those at once is a pretty fundamental shift.

I'd say where it's most mature today is on the small molecule side. Protein-ligand prediction in AlphaFold 3 was a big step up over the physics-based docking tools that people have been using for decades, and that's where we see the most immediate pull-through into actual programs. Antibodies and protein-protein interfaces are harder. They're flexible, the interfaces are large, antibody loops are notoriously difficult, and the data is thinner. The model has made progress there, but I'd be honest that it's not solved, and that's an area where we keep pushing.

The other thing I'd say is that structure prediction on its own is not drug discovery. It's a really powerful tool in the chain, but you still need to get from a structure to a molecule with the right properties, and you need to iterate, design, and learn from experiments. So the way I think about it, AlphaFold 3 gives you a kind of universal lens on biology at the atomic level, and then the real work at Isomorphic is building the rest of the engine around it, so that lens actually turns into medicines across whatever modality is right for the target.

r001.rationale: The response says one model can handle both small-molecule ligands binding in protein pockets and antibodies binding antigens, including their binding interfaces.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s exciting about AlphaFold 3 is the breadth of molecular interactions it can model. Drug discovery isn’t just about understanding a protein in isolation; it’s about understanding how you can interact with that protein to change what it does.

For small molecules, that means understanding how a compound binds to a target. For antibodies or other protein therapeutics, it means understanding protein–protein interactions. And the ability to model nucleic acids opens up another set of possibilities. So you have a common foundation that’s relevant across quite different therapeutic modalities.

The usefulness won’t necessarily be equal across all of those applications. A predicted structure doesn’t tell you everything about binding affinity, selectivity, or whether something will make an effective medicine. But it can give you a much better starting hypothesis for what to design and what to test. The opportunity is to put that into an iterative cycle with experiments, where each round helps you make better decisions about the next.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold 3 can model small molecules binding targets and antibody-related protein–protein interactions, but it does not clearly specify antibodies binding antigens.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing is the breadth. Drug discovery isn’t just about small molecules binding to proteins. You might be developing an antibody, a peptide, or something that interacts with DNA or RNA. Having a model that can reason about those different molecular components together gives you a much broader starting point.

The usefulness will vary by modality and by the question you’re asking. Sometimes you want to understand where a molecule binds; sometimes you want to understand the interface between two proteins, or how to make an interaction more specific. A predicted structure can give you a hypothesis to test and help you decide which experiments to run.

But that’s an important distinction: predicting a complex isn’t the same as predicting whether you have a successful drug. You still need to understand affinity, selectivity, what happens in a cell, and ultimately safety and efficacy. I see AlphaFold 3 as a powerful part of that discovery process, with applications across modalities, rather than something that solves all of those problems on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says the model covers small molecules binding proteins and mentions antibodies, but it does not clearly state that AlphaFold 3 models antibody–antigen interactions.
